\chapter{Evening}
\label{ch:hi-evening}
\hlchaptermodality{29}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say evening in Hindi and refuse the tempting but false link between \hi{शाम} and Sanskrit śyāmā.}

Say \hi{शाम}, reject the śyāmā resemblance as a false cognate, and pair it with \hi{सुबह} as two loans from the same source.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[shaam]{\hi{शाम} (shaam) — \textquotedblleft{}evening,\textquotedblright{} and a tempting false cognate}

\label{lesson:HI-C29-shaam}



\begin{quote}
Last lesson's \hi{सुबह} was Persian, not Sanskrit. This word is the same story — but this time there's a Sanskrit look-alike close enough to trip you up on purpose.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{शाम} — Persian again, not Sanskrit}
\textbf{\hi{शाम}} (\textbf{shaam}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{evening}\textquotedblright{} — is, like \emph{subah}, a genuine \textbf{Persian} loanword: from Persian \textbf{\ar{شام}} (\emph{šām}), which traces back through \textbf{Proto-Iranian} \emph{\textbf{*xšáfnyah}} to \textbf{Proto-Indo-Iranian} \emph{\textbf{*kšápā}} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{night}\textquotedblright{}). Hindi's two everyday time-words for \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}evening\textquotedblright{} both entered the language \textbf{via Persian}, not Sanskrit — though their deeper roots differ: \emph{subah}'s traces further back to \textbf{Arabic}, while \emph{shaam}'s is native \textbf{Indo-Iranian}, a sister branch to Sanskrit itself. Persian is what they share directly; their ultimate origins are not the same.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Be careful: a tempting, but FALSE, cognate}
Here's the trap: Sanskrit has its own word, \textbf{\hi{श्यामा}} (\textbf{śyāmā}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{dark, night-colored}\textquotedblright{}), that \emph{looks} like it should be \emph{shaam}'s cousin — similar sound, overlapping \textquotedblleft{}darkness/night\textquotedblright{} meaning, right in the neighborhood you'd expect. It \textbf{isn't}. \emph{Shaam} and \emph{śyāmā} trace to \textbf{two completely separate roots} that simply converged on similar sounds and meanings by coincidence — a genuine \textbf{false cognate}, not a shared one. Don't let the resemblance fool you into inventing a connection that isn't there.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}shaam\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}evening,\textquotedblright{} another genuine Persian loan
  \item the tempting trap — Sanskrit śyāmā looks related but ISN'T
  \item subah and shaam — both Persian, Hindi's whole \textquotedblleft{}morning and evening\textquotedblright{} pair borrowed from the same source language
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \hi{शाम} Sanskrit or Persian? (\textbf{Persian} — from \ar{شام}, śām, like subah.) Is \hi{शाम} related to Sanskrit \hi{श्यामा} (śyāmā, \textquotedblleft{}dark\textquotedblright{})? (\textbf{No} — a genuine false cognate; the resemblance is coincidental, not a shared root.) What do subah and shaam have in common, beyond both meaning a time of day? (\textbf{Both are Persian loanwords} — Hindi's morning/evening pair, unlike din/raat, isn't Sanskrit at all.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[e]{\hi{ए} — the vowel that had only ever been a mark}

\label{lesson:HI-S131-letter-e}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \textbf{\hi{◌े}} — what does it do to the consonant it sits on?

That mark has a \textbf{standing form}, and this is it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{ए}}
\textbf{\hi{ए}} — \emph{e}.

It is the \textbf{independent vowel}. The mark \textbf{\hi{◌े}} is what this sound looks like when it rides on a consonant; \textbf{\hi{ए}} is what it looks like when it stands on its own, with no consonant to attach to.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a long left stem joined to the descending tail
  \item a shorter right stem with an inward hook
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Script: two shapes, one sound}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you see} & \textbf{where it stands} \\
\midrule
\hi{◌े} & on a consonant \\
\hi{ए} & alone \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Every vowel in this script works this way, and you have met the arrangement twice before with \textbf{\hi{अ} / \hi{◌ा}} and with \textbf{\hi{उ} / \hi{◌ु}}. \textbf{A vowel sign and its letter are the same vowel in two postures}, and which one a word uses is decided by whether a consonant is there to carry it.

\textbf{\hi{ए}} turns up at the ends of words far more than at the beginnings, because that is where a vowel most often has nothing in front of it to ride on.

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{ए}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} descend the left stem, curve right through the lower shoulder, and sweep down through the tail without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and descend the shorter right stem into its inward hook
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2.} The pen comes up 2 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
Verified modern printed teaching form; everyday handwriting may simplify the curves.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Saurmandal, ‘Devanagari \hi{ए} stroke order.svg’, panels 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 5 August 2023.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at the mark and the letter side by side, and say what they share
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{◌े}  ·  \hi{ए}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{ए} three times, saying \emph{e} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Say it:} what decides which of the two a word uses
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What sound is \textbf{\hi{ए}}? (\emph{e}.) What is the sitting version of it? (\textbf{\hi{◌े}}.) What decides which one a word uses? (Whether there is a consonant for the vowel to ride on.)
\end{tcolorbox}
